lead: Mechanical diesel injection must create pressure high enough to atomise fuel and time delivery to a few crank degrees. Three mechanical layouts do this without electronics. The in-line jerk pump uses one plunger per cylinder. The distributor pump uses one plunger for all cylinders and sends fuel to each in turn. The unit injector puts the pump and nozzle together at the cylinder. Tractors, gensets, older trucks and large marine engines use them; the plunger-and-spill idea also sits inside modern high-pressure pumps.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 for the four jobs of an injection system — meter, atomise, distribute, time — and Unit 1 for four-stroke valve and injection timing.

blocks.text: The in-line jerk pump, called a plunger pump in some syllabi, has one pumping element per cylinder driven by one camshaft. On a four-stroke engine the pump camshaft turns at half engine speed, so each plunger injects once per two crank revolutions.

Each element is a plunger inside a barrel. Fuel fills the space above the plunger through an inlet port while the plunger is down. A vertical groove and a helical edge, the helix, are cut on the plunger. The helix sets the end of delivery.

items: The plunger covers the inlet port; trapped fuel cannot return to the gallery.
Pressure opens the delivery valve and the nozzle at its set pressure.
The helix uncovers the spill port; fuel spills back, pressure falls, and the delivery valve closes.
The plunger finishes its stroke without delivering, then returns.

blocks.text: Effective stroke s_eff is the plunger travel from port closing to spill opening. It is shorter than the total cam stroke. Volume per injection is the swept volume of that effective stroke:

blocks.where: V is fuel volume per injection (m³); d is plunger diameter (m); s_eff is effective stroke (m); π is 3.1416.

blocks.text: The control rack rotates the plunger to change fuel quantity. Rotation moves the helix relative to the spill port, so spill happens earlier or later; total stroke stays fixed. A delivery valve holds residual line pressure and stops backflow. Timing marks on the pump flange and flywheel set delivery start for cylinder one.
The distributor pump, or rotary pump, uses one plunger for all cylinders. The plunger reciprocates to pressurise fuel and rotates to direct fuel to each cylinder in turn.

A cam ring with one lobe per cylinder pushes rollers inward as the plunger rotates; each push gives one pumping stroke. The rotor outlet port lines up with each delivery union in firing order. A delivery valve at each union keeps the line filled.

A control sleeve or spill ring, moved by the governor, covers a spill port on the plunger. Moving the sleeve changes the spilled volume and so the delivered fuel. Small pumps may meter by inlet throttling instead.

items: Advantages: compact, one pumping element, fewer calibrations; common on 3 to 6 cylinder car and tractor engines.
Limits: one plunger supplies every cylinder, so maximum fuel and pressure are lower than a jerk pump.
Long high-pressure pipes add pressure lag and can make timing differ slightly between cylinders.
Wear in the rotor and cam ring upsets delivery balance.

blocks.text: The unit injector puts the pump and nozzle in one body at the cylinder head. The engine cam, through a rocker or a dedicated lobe, pushes the plunger directly. No long high-pressure pipe connects pump and nozzle.

The plunger pressurises fuel just above the nozzle needle. A helix or a spill valve ends injection; the rack or linkage sets fuel quantity. The nozzle opens at its set pressure and sprays into the chamber. Fuel lubricates the plunger and cools the body.

The short, stiff path gives fast pressure rise, precise timing and high pressure. Large marine and locomotive diesels use unit injectors. Limits: the camshaft and rocker carry the full injection load; the cylinder head is crowded; each unit needs setting; service costs more. Timing is set by the cam lobe, rocker clearance or shims, and marks on camshaft and flywheel.

All three pumps need static timing. Turn the engine to the specified angle before top dead centre on the compression stroke of cylinder one, align the pump or cam marks, then check dynamic timing by spill or strobe method. A wrong mark shifts every cylinder together.

Mechanical wear changes delivery, and there is no closed-loop correction. Pressure is limited by cam and plunger strength. Modern common rail separates pressure generation from injection timing — see Chapter 2.4.

figure.caption: The cam lifts the plunger; once the ports are covered, pressure opens the delivery valve and the nozzle injects. Notice that the helix, not the total cam stroke, decides when delivery ends.

examples.question: A jerk pump plunger has diameter 8 mm and effective stroke 3 mm. Find the fuel delivered per injection in m³ and in mm³. Take π = 3.1416.
steps: Convert: d = 8 mm = 0.008 m; s_eff = 3 mm = 0.003 m.
Convert to mm³: 1 m³ = 10⁹ mm³, so V = 1.508×10⁻⁷ × 10⁹ = 150.8 mm³.
examples.answer: The fuel delivered per injection is 1.508×10⁻⁷ m³, or 150.8 mm³.
examples.check:
import math
pi = 3.1416
d = 0.008
s_eff = 0.003
A = pi * d**2 / 4
V = A * s_eff
print(f'{A:.3e}')
print(f'{V:.3e}')
print(f'{V * 1e9:.1f}')

traps: Using total plunger stroke instead of effective stroke. The effective stroke starts only after the inlet and spill ports are covered by the plunger.
Thinking that rotating the plunger changes its stroke length. It changes the angular position of the helix, so the spill port opens earlier or later.
Confusing the delivery valve with the injector nozzle. The delivery valve is at the pump outlet and holds residual line pressure; the nozzle atomises fuel in the chamber.
Assuming a distributor pump feeds all cylinders at the same instant. The rotor lines up with one delivery union at a time in firing order.
Forgetting that a unit injector still needs timing marks. The cam lobe, rocker clearance or shims set injection timing even though there is no long high-pressure pipe.

quiz.q: What is the function of the helix on a jerk pump plunger?
quiz.a: The helix is the helical edge that uncovers the spill port. Its position relative to the spill port decides when delivery ends and therefore how much fuel is injected.

quiz.q: Why does rotating the plunger change fuel quantity but not the plunger stroke?
quiz.a: The cam fixes the total stroke. Rotation moves the helix around the plunger, so the spill port is uncovered earlier or later in the same stroke. The effective stroke from port closing to spill opening changes, while the total stroke remains constant.

quiz.q: A 6-cylinder engine uses a jerk pump with plunger diameter 7 mm and effective stroke 2.5 mm. Find the fuel delivered per injection in mm³. Take π = 3.1416.
quiz.a: Area = 3.1416 × 7² / 4 = 38.48 mm². Volume = 38.48 × 2.5 = 96.2 mm³. The fuel delivered per injection is about 96.2 mm³.

quiz.q: Compare a distributor pump and a unit injector for a 6-cylinder truck engine. Which one avoids long high-pressure pipes, and why does that matter?
quiz.a: The unit injector avoids long high-pressure pipes because the pump and nozzle are one unit at the cylinder head. Shorter pipe volume means faster pressure rise, less pressure lag, more precise timing and higher achievable injection pressure. The distributor pump needs a pipe to each cylinder, so pressure waves and small timing differences between cylinders are possible.

quiz.q: What does the delivery valve at a jerk pump outlet do?
quiz.a: It opens under pump pressure, then closes when pressure falls. It holds residual pressure in the high-pressure line and prevents fuel from flowing back into the pump between injections.

quiz.q: A four-stroke diesel engine runs at 2000 rpm. Its jerk pump camshaft turns at half engine speed. How many injections does one cylinder receive in one minute?
quiz.a: Pump camshaft speed = 2000 / 2 = 1000 rpm. Each plunger injects once per camshaft revolution, so injections per minute = 1000 for one cylinder.

quiz.q: Why is a distributor pump usually limited to smaller engines?
quiz.a: One plunger must supply all cylinders. As cylinder count and fuel demand rise, the single plunger must deliver more fuel per stroke and at higher pressure. That limits maximum fuel quantity and pressure compared with one plunger per cylinder.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern common-rail high-pressure pumps still use a cam-driven plunger and a spill valve; unit injectors survive in large marine engines and some locomotives. Electronic unit injectors replace the helix with a solenoid spill valve for ECU timing. Search for jerk pump phasing and calibration, distributor pump cam ring, and unit injector rocker adjustment. The pressure-control side appears in Chapter 2.4 and the electronic injector side in Chapter 2.5.
